comments.comment: Intuitively, stable optimization occurs when updates reinforce each other and gradually shift parameters toward a point of minimum loss. Instability therefore arises when updates overshoot, oscillate, or partially undo the progress made by previous steps~\cite{polyak1964methods, bertsekas1997nonlinear}. Understanding this behavior requires examining the mechanisms that govern how updates evolve from one iteration to the next. Two factors have traditionally played a central role in explaining these dynamics: the \textit{local curvature} of the loss landscape and the \textit{stochasticity} introduced by mini-batch sampling.

comments.selected_text: Training can be interpreted as a discrete-time dynamical system in which the local curvature of the loss function determines the stability of the updates [10], [11]. The curvature indicates how sensitive the loss is to parameter changes in different directions: when curvature is small, updates tend to produce smooth descent toward a minimum, whereas in directions of high curvature the same step can overshoot the minimum and induce oscillatory behavior [10], [11], [17]. For this reason, classical analyses of gradient descent relate stabil- ity to the spectrum of the Hessian of the loss function, whose eigenvalues quantify directional curvature and indicate how sensitive optimization is to the choice of learning rate [10], [11].

comments.selected_text: The break-even point framework of Jastrzebski et al. [12] is an attempt to extend the classical curvature-based stability condition to SGD. The central idea is to analyze stability along the sharpest direction of the loss landscape while explic- itly accounting for mini-batch stochasticity. Large s2 t means different mini- batches see substantially different local curvature, while small s2 t means they see similar curvature. In this sense, Eq. (6) can be read as a stochastic extension of the deterministic stability condition in Eq. (3), so that the first term captures curvature-induced amplification, while the second captures the destabilizing effect of mini-batch stochasticity. Under this definition, the break-even point is defined as the first iteration at which the left-hand side of Eq. (6) reaches 1. Intuitively, it marks the end of an early phase during which the choice of learning rate and batch size can strongly shape the later optimization trajectory. In this sense, a central conjecture of this framework is that, prior to this point, hyperparameters largely determine the maximum curvature and stochasticity levels encountered later in training, thereby setting the regime in which the subsequent dynamics unfold.

comments.selected_text: D. Practical Stability Analysis in Large-Model Pretraining Large-model training reports approach stability through observable symptoms and interventions on the training recipe. An instructive example is PaLM: Section 5.1 reports approx- imately 20 loss spikes during training of the 540B model despite global gradient clipping. The authors recovered by returning to a checkpoint about 100 steps before a spike and skipping 200–500 batches. Replaying those batches from a different parameter state did not reproduce the spikes, suggesting an interaction between data and model state rather than a property of the batches alone [24]. Reports accompanying released model weights provide fur- ther operational evidence. During OPT-175B training, loss divergence was associated with failures of the dynamic loss scale and growing final-layer activation norms. Recovery involved reducing the learning rate and restarting from an earlier checkpoint; lowering the gradient-clipping threshold from 1.0 to 0.3 also improved stability early in training [25]. These observations motivate monitoring the numerical state of training alongside the loss. OLMo 2 makes this diagnostic process explicit by measur- ing a rolling spike score on training loss and gradient norm, and using controlled ablations to study initialization, normal- ization, and optimizer settings. Its revised recipe combines global gradient clipping with changes including query–key normalization, reordered normalization, and a logit regular- izer (z-loss) [26]. In Llama 3, the authors report a stable pretraining recipe with few loss spikes and no interventions for divergence; they use learning-rate warmup and a staged batch- size schedule, and emphasize FP32 gradient accumulation and reduction for numerical stability [27]. These reports document both failure recovery and recipes that avoid recurrent failures, rather than a universal instability mechanism. Loss, gradient norm, and activation statistics are practical monitoring signals, but gradient magnitude alone does not describe the relationship between successive directions. A large gradient can reinforce or oppose its predecessor, and a sequence of individually bounded steps can still exhibit cumulative cancellation. We therefore seek a complementary description that can be computed from training gradients and interpreted through their temporal geometry. comments.selected_text: B. Noise Contribution under Mini-Batch Sampling Unbiased sampling does not make the noise interaction van- ish. Write gt−1 = ∇L(θt−2)+ξt−1. Fresh, conditionally unbi- ased batches give E[g⊤ t−1ξt] = 0 and E[∇L(θt−2)⊤ξt−1] = 0. With finite second moments, the preceding gradient contributes its own noise energy: E[g⊤ t−1(ξt −ξt−1)] = −E[∥ξt−1∥2] (17) Thus, even unbiased sampling noise contributes a systematic nonpositive term to the expected unnormalized interaction between consecutive gradients. This contribution is directly related to mini-batch size. Consider a mini-batch of b examples sampled uniformly without replacement from N > 1 training examples. Using the per-sample gradient covariance Σ(θ) defined in Eq. (5), the sampling variance satisfies E[∥ξt−1∥2] = N −b b(N −1)E[tr Σ(θt−2)]. (18) At fixed parameters, smaller batches produce larger sampling variance and, consequently, a larger negative expected noise contribution. For full-batch gradients (b = N), this contribu- tion vanishes. Noise can weaken directional coherence by enlarging gra- dient norms relative to their shared signal. For independent estimates at two fixed states, let µ, ν be the nonzero full gradients and vµ, vν the expected squared noise norms. When sampled norms concentrate, E[cos(µ + ξ, ν + ζ)] ≈ cos(µ, ν) (1 + vµ/∥µ∥2)(1 + vν/∥ν∥2) . This attenuation moves either sign toward zero. At the same fixed state, the common full-gradient direction gives the spe- cial case E[ρt] ≈ ∥∇L(θ)∥2 ∥∇L(θ)∥2 + N−b b(N−1) tr Σ(θ). (19) Here the expected cosine is nonnegative; the approximation quantifies the dilution of a common direction by sampling. During SGD, a sampled update also changes the next state, coupling noise and curvature. The fixed-state attenuation ar- gument therefore isolates a mechanism, while the batch-size intervention in Section IV-D tests its expression along evolving trajectories.

comments.selected_text: For constant-step plain SGD, the denominator represents the total distance traveled in parameter space, while the numerator measures the net displacement from initialization. Thus, RT quantifies the fraction of accumulated step length retained as net displacement. Using Eq. (10), this ratio satisfies R2 T = t=1 ∥gt∥2 + 2 1≤u<t≤T ∥gu∥∥gt∥ρu,t t=1 ∥gt∥ 2 . (21) Unlike ρt, which considers only adjacent gradients, RT incor- porates interactions across all temporal lags. When RT is near one, almost all traveled distance survives as net displacement; when it is near zero, little does. Repeated back-and-forth steps and weakly coherent sampled directions both suggest low retention. For example, equal-length orthogonal updates give RT = 1/ √ T, whereas equal opposing pairs cancel exactly. We therefore expect small RT when such behavior persists over a substantial part of an SGD path. Its value is relative to traveled distance: absolute displacement can still grow, and the sign of the complete interaction in Eq. (21) requires the full decomposition.

comments.comment: Some raw ideas (for you to polish):1. Condition for a loss spikeA loss spike occurs when\[\delta\mathcal L_{t-1}>0.\]Substituting,\[-\frac{\eta}{2}\|g_{t-1}\|^2-\frac{\eta}{2}\rho_t\|g_{t-1}\|\|g_t\|>0.\]For nonzero gradients, rearranging gives\[\boxed{\rho_t<-\frac{\|g_{t-1}\|}{\|g_t\|}}\]This is the condition for a loss increase under your second-order approximation.Equivalently, using the inner product,\[\boxed{g_{t-1}^\top g_t<-\|g_{t-1}\|^2.}\]2. What does this tell us?There are two necessary conditions:Condition A: Gradient reversalSince the right-hand side is negative,\[\rho_t<0.\]Thus, consecutive gradients must point in opposing directions (an angle greater than \(90^\circ\)).Condition B: Gradient magnitude increaseSince cosine similarity satisfies \(\rho_t\geq -1\), a loss spike is possible only if\[\boxed{\|g_t\|>\|g_{t-1}\|.}\]In other words, the gradient must grow in magnitude following the step, and the reversal must be sufficiently strong.3. Geometric interpretationLet \(\phi_t\) denote the angle between the two gradients. info.content: Some raw ideas (for you to polish):1. Condition for a loss spikeA loss spike occurs when\[\delta\mathcal L_{t-1}>0.\]Substituting,\[-\frac{\eta}{2}\|g_{t-1}\|^2-\frac{\eta}{2}\rho_t\|g_{t-1}\|\|g_t\|>0.\]For nonzero gradients, rearranging gives\[\boxed{\rho_t<-\frac{\|g_{t-1}\|}{\|g_t\|}}\]This is the condition for a loss increase under your second-order approximation.Equivalently, using the inner product,\[\boxed{g_{t-1}^\top g_t<-\|g_{t-1}\|^2.}\]2. What does this tell us?There are two necessary conditions:Condition A: Gradient reversalSince the right-hand side is negative,\[\rho_t<0.\]Thus, consecutive gradients must point in opposing directions (an angle greater than \(90^\circ\)).Condition B: Gradient magnitude increaseSince cosine similarity satisfies \(\rho_t\geq -1\), a loss spike is possible only if\[\boxed{\|g_t\|>\|g_{t-1}\|.}\]In other words, the gradient must grow in magnitude following the step, and the reversal must be sufficiently strong.3. Geometric interpretationLet \(\phi_t\) denote the angle between the two gradients. Then\[\cos\phi_t<-\frac{\|g_{t-1}\|}{\|g_t\|}.\]For example:Gradient magnitude ratio \(\|g_t\|/\|g_{t-1}\|\)	Required cosine similarity	Required angle1	\(\rho_t<-1\) (impossible)	—1.5	\(\rho_t<-0.667\)	\(>131.8^\circ\)2	\(\rho_t<-0.5\)	\(>120^\circ\)5	\(\rho_t<-0.2\)	\(>101.5^\circ\)10	\(\rho_t<-0.1\)	\(>95.7^\circ\)The larger the gradient magnitude increase, the less severe the directional reversal needs to be to produce a loss increase.

comments.selected_text: IV. EMPIRICAL CHARACTERIZATION OF GRADIENT INTERFERENCE We use full-batch GD to characterize directional overshoot, its effect on cumulative motion, and its coexistence with loss reduction. We then vary batch size to examine how sampling changes these signatures. The comparison covers a tanh MLP on 5,000 CIFAR-10 images, ResNet-32 on all 50,000 CIFAR-10 training images, and a word-level Transformer on WikiText-2. Each minimizes its complete fixed training objective for 3,000 updates at three constant learning rates (Table I). Within each model, rates share one frozen initialization and data preparation; they were selected by earlier training calibrations to expose contrasting dynamics, without test-loss selection. Plain GD uses no momentum, weight decay, clipping or schedule. These comparisons test whether the same geometric signatures recur across the three objectives; they do not isolate architecture ef- fects. Appendix B specifies objectives, architectures, precision and measurement details.
